title: Unit 10: Macro Economics I
subtitle: The big picture and the business cycle

questions.prompt: What does macroeconomics study?
choices: The economy as a whole — things like a country's total output, inflation, and jobs
Only how one family budgets its monthly income
How to pick a single winning stock
The payroll rules inside one small company
questions.explanation: Macroeconomics zooms out to the whole economy — total production, prices, and employment — instead of one person or business.

questions.prompt: Microeconomics looks at individual choices (one person or business), while macroeconomics looks at the whole economy.
questions.explanation: Micro means the small, individual scale; macro means the big, whole-economy scale.

questions.prompt: Match each question to whether it is a micro or a macro question.
pairs: Should I buy a $5 coffee or save it?
Is the whole country's unemployment rising?
Should this bakery raise its bread price?
Is inflation across the nation speeding up?
questions.explanation: Personal or single-business choices are micro; nationwide totals like inflation and unemployment are macro.

questions.prompt: Which of these are macroeconomic topics? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: A nation's total economic output (GDP)
The country's overall inflation rate
Which sneakers you should buy this week
The national unemployment rate
questions.explanation: GDP, inflation, and unemployment describe the whole economy. Your sneaker choice is a personal, micro decision.

questions.prompt: Sort each topic into microeconomics or macroeconomics.
questions.explanation: One person, family, or business is micro. Whole-country totals are macro.

questions.prompt: Across a whole economy, what usually happens to prices when total demand for goods rises much faster than businesses can produce them?
choices: Prices tend to rise (upward pressure on prices)
Prices fall all the way to zero
Prices can never change
The economy instantly shuts down
questions.explanation: Just like in a single market, when economy-wide demand outruns supply, prices get pushed up.

questions.prompt: Even though it studies the whole economy, macroeconomics still uses the ideas of supply and demand — just at a much larger scale.
questions.explanation: Supply and demand work for one lemonade stand and for an entire country's economy alike.

questions.prompt: What does GDP (Gross Domestic Product) measure?
choices: The total value of all goods and services a country produces in a period
The total number of people living in a country
How much cash the government keeps in the bank
The price of a single company's stock
questions.explanation: GDP adds up the value of everything a country produces — it's the main scoreboard for the size of an economy.

questions.prompt: When GDP is growing, the economy is producing more goods and services than before.
questions.explanation: Rising GDP means more output — usually a sign of an expanding, healthier economy.

questions.prompt: An economy is said to be in a contraction (or recession) when...
choices: Its GDP is shrinking — total output is falling
Its GDP is growing quickly
Prices become perfectly stable
Everyone suddenly gets a raise
questions.explanation: A contraction means the economy is shrinking — GDP falls instead of grows.

questions.prompt: A country's GDP grows from $1,000 billion to $1,030 billion in a year. What is the growth rate?
questions.explanation: The increase is $30 billion; $30 ÷ $1,000 = 0.03 = 3% growth.

questions.prompt: Sort each situation into growth or contraction.
items: Factories produce more cars than last year
GDP falls for six months straight
More new businesses open and hire
Output drops and shops cut back
questions.explanation: More output is growth; falling output is contraction.

questions.prompt: Which of these count toward this year's GDP? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: A new car built and sold this year
A haircut you paid for this year
A used car resold from five years ago
A fresh loaf of bread baked and sold this year
questions.explanation: GDP counts new goods and services produced this period. Reselling an old used car isn't new production, so it doesn't add to GDP.

questions.prompt: Using the Rule of 72, if GDP grows about 3% per year, roughly how many years does the economy take to double in size?
questions.explanation: 72 ÷ 3 = 24, so at 3% annual growth an economy roughly doubles in about 24 years.

questions.prompt: What is inflation?
choices: A general rise in the prices of goods and services over time
A drop in the price of everything
The total number of jobs in a country
The interest a bank pays you
questions.explanation: Inflation is the overall upward drift of prices — the same dollar buys a little less each year.

questions.prompt: During inflation, a dollar buys less than it used to — its purchasing power falls.
questions.explanation: When prices rise, each dollar stretches less far, so your money's purchasing power shrinks.

questions.prompt: What is the Consumer Price Index (CPI) used for?
choices: Tracking the average price of a typical basket of goods and services over time
Counting how many people have jobs
Measuring a single company's profit
Setting the price of gold
questions.explanation: The CPI follows the cost of a common basket of everyday items, so it's a key gauge of inflation.

questions.prompt: In many countries, central banks aim for an inflation rate of about 2% per year.
questions.explanation: A low, steady ~2% is seen as healthy — enough to keep the economy moving without eroding money too fast.

questions.prompt: Your savings earned a 5% nominal return this year, but inflation was 2%. What was your approximate real return?
questions.explanation: Real return is roughly nominal return minus inflation: 5% − 2% = 3%. That's your gain in actual buying power.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The general rise in prices over time
How much your money can actually buy
An index tracking the price of a basket of goods
questions.explanation: These four ideas explain how rising prices quietly shrink the value of money.

questions.prompt: A basket of goods cost $100 last year. With 2% inflation, what does that same basket cost this year?
questions.explanation: 2% of $100 is $2, so the basket now costs $100 + $2 = $102.

questions.prompt: What does the unemployment rate measure?
choices: The percentage of the labor force who want a job but don't have one
The total number of people in the country
How much money workers earn
The number of companies that exist
questions.explanation: It's the share of people who are actively looking for work but can't find it, out of everyone in the labor force.

questions.prompt: In a labor force of 200 people, 10 are unemployed and looking for work. What is the unemployment rate?
questions.explanation: 10 ÷ 200 = 0.05 = 5%. Unemployment rate is unemployed people divided by the labor force.

questions.prompt: A small amount of unemployment is normal, because people are always switching jobs or just entering the workforce.
questions.explanation: Some 'frictional' unemployment is healthy — it just means people are moving between jobs. Zero unemployment almost never happens.

questions.prompt: When unemployment rises sharply, what tends to happen? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: People have less income to spend
Overall consumer spending tends to fall
Everyone instantly gets richer
Businesses may sell less and slow down
questions.explanation: Fewer paychecks means less spending, which can ripple out and slow the whole economy.

questions.prompt: Match each type of unemployment to an example.
pairs: Someone quit to search for a better job
People laid off during a recession
A worker's skills no longer match available jobs
questions.explanation: Frictional is between jobs; cyclical follows the business cycle; structural is a mismatch of skills or industries.

questions.prompt: An unemployment rate of exactly 0% is the normal, healthy goal for every economy.
questions.explanation: Some unemployment is always expected as people switch jobs; economists aim for low unemployment, not zero.

questions.prompt: A full-time student who is not looking for work is counted as...
choices: Not in the labor force, so not counted as unemployed
Unemployed
Employed
The main cause of inflation
questions.explanation: To be 'unemployed' you must be actively looking for work. People not seeking a job aren't in the labor force at all.

questions.prompt: Put the four phases of the business cycle in order, starting from a growing economy.
questions.explanation: The economy grows (expansion), tops out (peak), shrinks (contraction), and bottoms out (trough) — then it starts over.

questions.prompt: Match each business-cycle phase to its description.
pairs: The economy is growing and jobs are rising
Growth tops out at its highest point
The economy shrinks and output falls
The low point before growth begins again
questions.explanation: These four phases repeat over and over — that's why it's called a cycle.

questions.prompt: The business cycle always turns — no expansion lasts forever, and no contraction lasts forever either.
questions.explanation: Booms eventually cool and downturns eventually recover — the cycle keeps turning.

questions.prompt: A recession is another name for which phase of the business cycle?
choices: A contraction, when the economy is shrinking
A peak, when growth is highest
An expansion, when the economy is growing
A trough that lasts only one day
questions.explanation: A recession is a significant, sustained contraction — falling output across the economy.

questions.prompt: Which are typical signs of an economic expansion? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Rising GDP
Falling unemployment
Widespread layoffs and shrinking output
Growing consumer spending
questions.explanation: During an expansion, output, jobs, and spending all tend to rise. Widespread layoffs signal a contraction instead.

questions.prompt: Sort each event into the expansion or contraction phase.
questions.explanation: Growth, hiring, and rising spending mark an expansion; falling output and layoffs mark a contraction.

questions.prompt: The lowest point of the business cycle, just before the economy starts to recover, is called the...
choices: Trough
Peak
Expansion
Boom
questions.explanation: The trough is the bottom — the turning point where a contraction ends and a new expansion begins.

questions.prompt: Macroeconomics is best described as the study of...
choices: The whole economy — output, inflation, and jobs
One family's weekly budget
A single company's logo design
How to trade one stock
questions.explanation: Macro zooms out to the entire economy, unlike micro's focus on individuals and single businesses.

questions.prompt: GDP measures the total value of goods and services a country produces.
questions.explanation: It's the main scoreboard for the size of an economy.

questions.prompt: GDP rises from $2,000 billion to $2,040 billion in a year. What is the growth rate?
questions.explanation: The $40 increase ÷ $2,000 = 0.02 = 2% growth.

questions.prompt: During inflation, the purchasing power of your money...
choices: Falls — each dollar buys less
Rises — each dollar buys more
Stays perfectly constant
Becomes infinite
questions.explanation: Rising prices mean your money buys fewer goods, so purchasing power falls.

questions.prompt: You earn a 6% nominal return while inflation is 2%. What is your approximate real return?
questions.explanation: Real return is roughly nominal minus inflation: 6% − 2% = 4%.

questions.prompt: If 8 people are unemployed in a labor force of 100, what is the unemployment rate?
Order the business cycle phases, starting from a growing economy.
questions.explanation: Grow, top out, shrink, bottom out — then the cycle repeats.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Total value of everything a country produces
An index tracking the price of a basket of goods
A period when the economy is shrinking
The low point before the economy recovers
questions.explanation: These are the core macro terms from this unit.

questions.prompt: Which of these are macroeconomic measures? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: National GDP
The countrywide inflation rate
Which cereal you eat for breakfast
The national unemployment rate
questions.explanation: GDP, inflation, and unemployment describe the whole economy; your cereal is a personal choice.

questions.prompt: Sort each into expansion or contraction.
questions.explanation: Rising output and jobs mean expansion; falling output and layoffs mean contraction.
